clue.text: It's irritating, the rise of this luminary

indicators.note: in a down entry a rise reads the word from the bottom up, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: 'Rats!' is the exclamation of someone irritated

explanation.surface: A celebrity's rise to fame is getting on someone's nerves.
explanation.definitionFit: A luminary is a famous or eminent person, a celebrity, which is what a star is.

clue.text: 5's 10 8 who riles press, no worries, drinking Australia dry

definitions.note: Humphries's Cultural Attache, his boorish comic character

indicators.note: the reshuffled letters take in the other pieces, as a drinker takes in liquid
worrying at something pulls it about, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
TT is teetotal, abstaining from drink

explanation.surface: An Australian diplomat annoys the newspapers, and with typical Aussie nonchalance he drinks the country dry.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-references read HUMPHRIES's CULTURAL ATTACHE: Sir Les Patterson was Barry Humphries's crude diplomat character. 'No worries' is the Australian catchphrase, but 'worries' alone signals the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Barry Humphries created Sir Les Patterson, a vulgar Australian Minister for the Arts posted abroad as a diplomat.

clue.text: Cobber will ring to say G'day

parts.note: a cobber is Australian slang for a mate, and here simply a man, he
will contracts to 'll, as in he'll
a ring is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: An Australian mate will phone up to say good day.
explanation.walkthrough: HE'LL, the cobber will, has a ring added. Cobber and G'day are both Australian slang, matching the Humphries theme.
explanation.definitionFit: G'day is the Australian greeting, a casual way of saying hi to someone.

clue.text: Plant of purple hue is in need of water, I fancy

indicators.note: the word is goes into the middle of the other letters, as though in their keeping
fancy as an adjective means elaborate or reworked, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener thinks a purple-flowered plant is wilting and needs watering.
explanation.definitionFit: Wisteria is a climbing shrub bearing hanging clusters of lilac or violet blossoms.

clue.text: Our Barry Cryer's regulars want his instead, following hunch

indicators.note: the altered name comes after the piece for hunch

parts.note: a hunch is a hump on the back

indicators.note: instead means in place of, so each regular letter is replaced
the letters of his are wanted in those places, one for each regular letter
the regular letters of the name are its first, third and fifth, the ones to be swapped

parts.note: the comedian Barry Cryer's surname

explanation.surface: A tribute to the comedian Barry Cryer, oddly asking that someone else be put in his place.
explanation.walkthrough: Barry Cryer and Barry Humphries were both British-loved comedians; in CRYER the letters C, Y and R in odd positions become H, I and S, giving HRIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Barry Humphries is the Australian comedian behind Dame Edna, here claimed fondly as 'our' Barry.

clue.text: Across this base are old women stalking with spears

indicators.note: the inner letters pierce the word this and its base, as a spear goes into a body

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the women walk with the old verb, keeping close to it

parts.note: art is the archaic form of are, as in 'thou art'
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A tribal scene: women armed with spears stalk prey across an old camp.
explanation.walkthrough: W is the abbreviation for women and also for with.
explanation.definitionFit: Thwartwise is an old adverb meaning crosswise or transversely, lying athwart something.

clue.text: In hall, I've won husband that's ineffectual?

definitions.note: 'House!' is the call of a winning bingo player in a bingo hall

parts.note: something ineffectual is of no use: O, a zero for no, then USE

explanation.surface: A wife in a hall announces a victory over a husband who is good for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: In bingo a player who completes the card shouts 'House!', meaning I've won.
explanation.definitionFit: In a bingo hall, the winner calls out this word to claim the prize for a full card.

clue.text: American college dons attending specific case

parts.note: attending a place is being at it

indicators.note: to don is to put on, so the definite article wears the other letters inside it

parts.note: the is the definite article, the specific one

explanation.surface: University teachers in America attend to a particular legal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like college tutors but is the verb, put on.
explanation.definitionFit: An attache case is a slim briefcase for documents, named after the diplomatic attache.

clue.text: Misleading act leads to university place

parts.note: a lie is a deliberately misleading statement or act

indicators.note: leads to points at the opening letter of the word university

explanation.surface: A deceitful stunt gets someone a place at university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads to' takes just the first letter of university.
explanation.definitionFit: As in the phrase meaning instead of, it denotes stead or substitution, a borrowing from French.

clue.text: Aesthetic selection includes a course on reflection

indicators.note: the word for selection holds the next pieces inside it

parts.note: a cull is a selective removal, from select

indicators.note: reflected in a mirror, these letters appear back to front

parts.note: a rut is a fixed track or course

explanation.surface: An arty selection of courses is reconsidered.
explanation.definitionFit: Cultural concerns the arts and taste, as aesthetic matters do.

clue.text: Who's sharing spliff with one retired PC?

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the phrase reads backwards

parts.note: a smoker sharing a joint with someone is a pot pal, pot being cannabis

explanation.surface: A retired police constable is caught sharing a joint.
explanation.walkthrough: PC looks like police constable, given 'retired' and a spliff; it is a personal computer.
explanation.definitionFit: A PC, a personal computer, includes the portable kind used on the knees.

clue.text: On top of which, orang-utan's back in trailer

definitions.note: a phrase meaning moreover, as the conjunction can

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the advertisement

parts.note: a trailer advertises a film, so it is an ad

indicators.note: the back of the word is its final letter

parts.note: the ape's name, of which only the back is used

explanation.surface: An orang-utan's rear end appears in a film trailer.
explanation.definitionFit: The conjunction adds one thing to another, as 'on top of which' or moreover does.

clue.text: Change that makes bare barn a place of education

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as an instruction: turning bare into barn swaps its E for N
second meaning: ... College, the famous English public school

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: written out, the change from bare to barn is 'E to N', and those letters run together spell the school.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton is the English boarding school near Windsor, an institution where pupils are taught.

clue.text: Among those receiving not a morsel of food, starving Oliver calls for more

indicators.note: the emptied name goes in among the other letters
the letter is taken away from the word

parts.note: fences are receivers of stolen goods

indicators.note: a morsel is a small bite, here just the first letter

parts.note: only the first letter of food is wanted

indicators.note: starving empties the name, leaving only its outside letters

parts.note: the name with its middle starved away leaves its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Oliver Twist, hungry among workhouse boys getting no food, asks for more.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Twist famously asked for more; FENCES fits his Dickensian world of Fagin.
explanation.definitionFit: Encores are an audience's shouts for an extra performance, demands for more.

clue.text: Harsh dictator's cross

indicators.note: a dictator here is one who dictates aloud, so the word is as spoken

parts.note: a rood is a crucifix, a cross

explanation.surface: A tyrant is cross and harsh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' wants to be a tyrant; it is a person dictating, speaking words aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Rude can mean rough or harsh, as in a rude awakening.

clue.text: Pressure to abandon ship? Take painter

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it, so the ship's letters leave the word for pressure

parts.note: duress is pressure or coercion
SS is a steamship
R, recipe, is Latin for take on a prescription

explanation.surface: Under pressure to abandon ship, someone grabs a painter, the rope on a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Painter' suggests the rope used to tie up a boat, in keeping with the ship; it is the artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Albrecht Durer was the German Renaissance artist known for engravings and woodcuts.

clue.text: Little capital put away in a blast

indicators.note: the word for put away goes inside the other letters

parts.note: 'Blast!' and 'Damn!' are both mild curses
to stow is to pack away

explanation.surface: A small amount of money is lost in an explosion.
explanation.walkthrough: Adamstown is the capital of the Pitcairn Islands, home to only a few dozen people, hence 'little'.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamstown is the tiny seat of government of Pitcairn, one of the world's smallest capitals.

clue.text: Balls up

definitions.meaning: in cricket an ... is a set of six balls bowled
finished, as when time is up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls up' reads as a British slang phrase for a mess; it is two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: An over is the cricket unit of six deliveries, and over also means ended or finished.

clue.text: Corrupt hosts need a comic — possibly 5's 7 31 12 25 1

definitions.note: Humphries's housewife and superstar, the billing Dame Edna gave herself

indicators.note: the word for corrupt plays host to the other letters inside it

parts.note: to corrupt data is to damage it

indicators.note: comic means funny, and funny letters are oddly arranged

parts.note: taken as written
ever as in 'could you ever?', where it softens to possibly

explanation.surface: Crooked hosts of a show are in want of a comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-references read HUMPHRIES's HOUSEWIFE AND SUPERSTAR: Dame Edna Everage, Barry Humphries's character from Melbourne's suburbs, called herself a housewife superstar.
explanation.definitionFit: Barry Humphries created Dame Edna as a Melbourne homemaker who became a glamorous stage celebrity.

clue.text: Work done, assuming male hasn't fiddled around

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go around the next word
fiddled means tampered with, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: if means assuming, on condition that

explanation.surface: A worker claims the job is done, provided the man hasn't cooked the books.
explanation.definitionFit: A man-shift is a unit of labour: the work done by one person during one shift.

clue.text: In a cycle of depression, I muddle through

indicators.note: the letter I goes into the cycled word
cycling moves the first letter round to the end

parts.note: a trough is a depression or low point

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in a recurring bout of depression struggles on.
explanation.definitionFit: To rough it is to manage with hardship and few comforts, struggling on regardless.

clue.text: Rashford & co "soft"? Grow a pair!

definitions.note: a crude idiom telling someone to show courage

parts.note: Marcus Rashford played for Manchester United, Man U for short
p is piano, soft in music

explanation.surface: A fan taunts Rashford and teammates as soft and tells them to toughen up.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases urge someone to stop being weak and show courage.

clue.text: Oh, I forgot to tell you about Chambers

indicators.note: the postscript goes around the letter

parts.note: a PS, postscript, adds what the writer forgot
O is the exclamation oh

explanation.surface: Someone suddenly remembers to mention the Chambers dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: Chambers suggests the dictionary beloved of crossword setters; a po is a chamber pot.
explanation.definitionFit: Po is British slang for a chamber pot, and these are several of them.

clue.text: Features of trousers which are surprisingly lucky

definitions.meaning: folded hems at the bottom of trouser legs
unexpected strokes of luck, as in 'a turn-up for the books'

explanation.walkthrough: 'A turn-up for the books' is British for a surprising, often welcome event.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both turned-back hems on trousers and unexpected fortunate events.

clue.text: The compiling team turned up a great!

indicators.note: in a down entry this reads from the bottom upwards

parts.note: the setters as a team are us
per means a, as in five pounds a head

explanation.surface: The setters arrive and are greeted as great.
explanation.definitionFit: Super is an exclamation of enthusiasm, like 'great!'.

clue.text: When to articulate wishes in some parts?

indicators.note: articulating is saying aloud, so the word is as spoken
only in some regional accents do these words sound alike

parts.note: wants means wishes

explanation.surface: Someone asks when to voice their wishes in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: In some accents 'wants' is said much like 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: Once means at one time, answering the question when.

clue.text: Somewhat jaunty persona of certain conductors

indicators.note: just part of the phrase supplies the letters

parts.note: the letters run across the end of jaunty and the start of persona

explanation.surface: A cheerful public image belongs to some orchestra conductors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductors' suggests orchestras; it is semiconductors, where n-type material carries negative charge.
explanation.definitionFit: N-type semiconductors carry current mainly by electrons, so the label describes certain conductors.

clue.text: So many cross-dressers, say, Norton or Ross?

parts.note: TV is short for transvestite
a host is a great number

explanation.surface: Speculation that famous chat-show hosts draw a crowd of cross-dressers.
explanation.walkthrough: Graham Norton and Jonathan Ross host British television chat shows.
explanation.definitionFit: Graham Norton and Jonathan Ross are both presenters of television chat shows.

clue.text: Spooner's water-pipe is reopening fruits of the garden

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the initial sounds of words

parts.note: a hose is a flexible water pipe
rips means tears open again

explanation.surface: A garden hose is splitting open again.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosehips are the red fruits of the rose that follow the flowers.

clue.text: Dubious adopting primer for mental arithmetic

definitions.note: a mass noun for calculations, matching the plural answer

indicators.note: the word takes the letter in, as a family adopts a child

parts.note: sus is slang for suspicious or dubious

indicators.note: a primer comes first, so this is the first letter

parts.note: the first letter of mental

explanation.surface: A questionable textbook for teaching mental arithmetic is taken up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primer' looks like a school book; it is the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing sums is doing arithmetic: calculations with numbers.

clue.text: Man's one female for keeping!

indicators.note: the word for us holds the other letters, keeping them inside

parts.note: man in the sense of humankind is us, we
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A man declares the one woman he means to keep for good.
explanation.walkthrough: As a whole the clue also defines the answer: a man's one woman, kept for life. With 7 it gives HOUSEWIFE, Dame Edna's proud boast.
explanation.definitionFit: A married man's spouse is the one woman he commits to permanently.

clue.text: The person unfortunately carrying master's measuring equipment

indicators.note: the scrambled letters carry the abbreviation inside them
unfortunate letters have met with an accident and are scrambled

parts.note: M for master

explanation.surface: Someone unluckily lugs about the boss's instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Phon meters are instruments for measuring loudness in phons, units of perceived sound level.
